articles.title: Mastering LINQ in C#: 12 Practical Examples Every .NET Developer Should Know
articles.excerpt: If you're a .NET developer, you've probably written countless for and foreach loops to filter, search, sort, and transform collections. Before LINQ (Language Integrated Query) was introduced in .NET 3…
articles.body: If you're a .NET developer, you've probably written countless for and foreach loops to filter, search, sort, and transform collections. Before LINQ (Language Integrated Query) was introduced in .NET 3.5, developers had to write repetitive looping logic for almost every data operation. While those approaches still work, they often make the code longer, harder to read, and more difficult to maintain. LINQ changed that by introducing a clean, expressive, and powerful way to query data directly within C#. Whether you're working with: Lists Arrays Dictionaries XML Entity Framework Core SQL Server APIs LINQ is one of the most valuable features you can master.

articles.title: The Hidden Job Market: Why Thousands of Open Roles Never Show Up in Your Job Search
articles.excerpt: When people search for jobs today, they usually start with Google, LinkedIn, Indeed, or another large job board. There is an assumption that these platforms provide a reasonably complete picture of wh…
articles.body: When people search for jobs today, they usually start with Google, LinkedIn, Indeed, or another large job board. There is an assumption that these platforms provide a reasonably complete picture of what companies are hiring for. In reality, that assumption is far from true. A significant number of open positions never become visible through these channels, even though they are publicly accessible on the internet. Over the last few months, while building WorkWay , I spent a lot of time looking at how companies publish jobs and how those jobs are discovered. One pattern became increasingly obvious. Modern companies rarely manage job listings themselves.

articles.title: Why you don't need a perfectly clear sky to enjoy the total solar eclipse on Aug. 12
articles.excerpt: Millions will see a deep partial or total solar eclipse on Aug. 12, but there's no need to fixate on completely clear skies.
articles.body: Are you ready for the eclipse? Whether you're bound for the path of totality or set to see a partial eclipse from Europe, Canada or the northeast U.S. on Wednesday, Aug. 12, there's a dirty word eclipse chasers hate to utter during an eclipse season, and yet become completely obsessed with — clouds. Related: Total solar eclipse 2026 — Everything you need to know We all start behaving as though Earth's atmosphere owes us something. After spending years studying the climate and where it is most likely along a path of totality to have a clear sky, we're in position and can now do almost nothing about it save for drive or sail a few miles. We refresh cloud forecasts. We compare satellite imagery. We point at scraps of blue sky as if we can persuade them to remain so at a specific time.

articles.title: 'One more step': NASA astronauts conduct 6.5-hour spacewalk to prep ISS for solar array upgrade
articles.excerpt: Jessica Meir and Anil Menon completed a 6.5-hour spacewalk to install solar array mounting hardware outside of the International Space Station on Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026.
articles.body: Two NASA astronauts installed the seventh and final set of mounting hardware for new sets of solar arrays during a successful 6.5-hour spacewalk outside of the International Space Station. Jessica Meir and Anil Menon on Thursday (Aug. 6), assembled the modification kit for one of the space station's eight power channels, which will allow for the future addition of a new ISS Rolll-Out Solar Array (iROSA). Since 2021, astronauts on prior spacewalks have deployed six of the iROSA assemblies, leaving now just two awaiting delivery to the station later this year. Like building a giant erector set, Meir and Menon worked to assemble and bolt together the triangular brackets on the 3B power channel, located on the far right, or starboard (S6) segment of the station's backbone truss.
